Section 1.1: Thinking Like a Physicist

Learning Target: Students will explain how physics uses observation, measurement, evidence, models, and testable claims to understand the natural world.

WTC

WTC 1

U1-11-0001 · WTC · 1.1 · U1-S1-IC3 · DOK 3 · wtc-shared-physics-context

A class investigates why a toy car sometimes travels farther after the same push. They record distances, note that the floor feels different in two lanes, and propose two explanations. Identify one observation, one inference, and one testable claim the class could make. Then explain what additional evidence would help decide between the explanations.

Answer / solution

A valid response distinguishes measured/observed facts from interpretations, proposes a claim tied to measurable variables, and names evidence that could support or challenge competing explanations.

Alignment / evidence

Learning Target: Students will explain how physics uses observation, measurement, evidence, models, and testable claims to understand the natural world.

I Can: I can use evidence from a short scenario to decide whether a physics explanation is supported and explain why formulas in physics are guides for thinking, not just tools for calculation.

Representation: phenomenon + verbal/model reasoning

Evidence job: U1-EP-0001 mapped to U1-MG01

Source basis: Hewitt Ch. 1 conceptual-method source packet

Notes Example

Notes Example 1

U1-11-0002 · Notes Example · 1.1 · U1-S1-IC1 · DOK 1 · sci-knowledge-claim-classification

A reference statement summarizes a repeatedly observed relationship between two measured quantities without explaining the mechanism. Should it be described as a scientific law or a scientific theory?

Answer / solution

Scientific law; a law summarizes a consistent relationship, while a theory provides an explanatory framework.

Alignment / evidence

Learning Target: Students will explain how physics uses observation, measurement, evidence, models, and testable claims to understand the natural world.

I Can: I can distinguish between an observation, inference, hypothesis, law, and theory.

Representation: verbal explanation/context

Evidence job: U1-EP-0002 mapped to U1-MG01

Source basis: Framework U1-S1 section reference packet

Notes Example 2

U1-11-0004 · Notes Example · 1.1 · U1-S1-IC2 · DOK 2 · testable-scientific-claim

Focus on whether an observation could support or challenge the claim. A claim about motion can be tested only after the reference frame and measurable outcome are specified. Explain why those details matter.

Answer / solution

They make the claim unambiguous and connect it to observations that different investigators can compare.

Alignment / evidence

Learning Target: Students will explain how physics uses observation, measurement, evidence, models, and testable claims to understand the natural world.

I Can: I can explain why a claim must be testable to be scientific.

Representation: verbal explanation/context

Evidence job: U1-EP-0004 mapped to U1-MG01

Source basis: Hewitt Ch. 1 conceptual-method source packet

Notes Example 3

U1-11-0006 · Notes Example · 1.1 · U1-S1-IC3 · DOK 2 · evidence-model-meaning

A student treats a formula as a button sequence and cannot explain what any symbol represents. What important role of a physics equation is being missed?

Answer / solution

An equation is a model of a relationship among physical quantities and should communicate how those quantities are connected, not only produce a number.

Alignment / evidence

Learning Target: Students will explain how physics uses observation, measurement, evidence, models, and testable claims to understand the natural world.

I Can: I can use evidence from a short scenario to decide whether a physics explanation is supported and explain why formulas in physics are guides for thinking, not just tools for calculation.

Representation: verbal explanation/context

Evidence job: U1-EP-0006 mapped to U1-MG01

Source basis: Unit 1 Assessment Plan §1.1

Notes Example 4

U1-11-0008 · Notes Example · 1.1 · U1-S1-IC3 · DOK 2 · evidence-model-meaning

A learner says, ‘The equation proves the object must behave that way, even if the measurements disagree.’ Critique the statement.

Answer / solution

Equations are models based on assumptions and evidence. If reliable measurements disagree, the assumptions, measurements, or model must be examined.

Alignment / evidence

Learning Target: Students will explain how physics uses observation, measurement, evidence, models, and testable claims to understand the natural world.

I Can: I can use evidence from a short scenario to decide whether a physics explanation is supported and explain why formulas in physics are guides for thinking, not just tools for calculation.

Representation: verbal explanation/context

Evidence job: U1-EP-0008 mapped to U1-MG01

Source basis: Framework U1-S1 section reference packet

Notes You Try It 4

U1-11-0009 · Notes You Try It · 1.1 · U1-S1-IC3 · DOK 2 · evidence-model-meaning

A relationship is written as speed = distance/time. Explain what the relationship says physically before using any numbers.

Answer / solution

It says speed compares how much distance is covered with the time taken; more distance in the same time means greater speed, and the same distance in more time means lower speed.

A class notices condensation on the outside of a cold cup and writes, ‘Water vapor from the air changed to liquid.’ Is that sentence an observation or an inference? Explain the distinction.

Answer / solution

Inference; it explains the observed droplets rather than merely reporting what was directly observed.

Answer / solution

Measurements vary; a supported explanation should fit the overall evidence and account for reasonable uncertainty rather than require every value to be identical.

A cart is released from the same ramp height five times. Its travel times are 2.1 s, 2.0 s, 2.2 s, 2.1 s, and 2.0 s. A student claims, ‘The cart takes about 2.1 s under these conditions.’ Decide whether the evidence supports the claim and explain why.

Answer / solution

Yes. The repeated measurements cluster closely around 2.1 s, so the claim matches the evidence within the observed variation.

U1-11-0079 · Practice Set 3 · 1.1 · U1-S1-IC3 · DOK 2 · evidence-model-meaning

Section 1.2: Forces and Newton’s First Law

Learning Target: Students will explain Newton’s First Law and use the idea of inertia to predict whether an object’s motion will stay the same or change.

WTC

WTC 1

U1-12-0136 · WTC · 1.2 · U1-S2-IC1 · DOK 3 · wtc-shared-physics-context

A bus moves straight at steady speed, then brakes. A backpack on the floor slides forward relative to the bus while a seated student feels the seat belt pull. Use Newton’s First Law to explain the backpack’s motion, identify whether inertia is a force, and describe the forces that act on a backpack resting on the floor before braking.

Answer / solution

Before braking, zero net force is consistent with steady motion. Inertia is a property, not a force. Weight and the floor’s support force act vertically; during braking, a horizontal interaction changes the backpack’s motion.

Alignment / evidence

Learning Target: Students will explain Newton’s First Law and use the idea of inertia to predict whether an object’s motion will stay the same or change.

I Can: I can state Newton’s First Law in everyday language.

Representation: phenomenon + verbal/model reasoning

Evidence job: U1-EP-0136 mapped to U1-MG02

Source basis: Hewitt §§2.3/2.6 Newton I/support-force source packet

Notes Example 1

U1-12-0137 · Notes Example · 1.2 · U1-S2-IC1 · DOK 2 · newton-first-law-prediction

An air-hockey puck is already moving. A student says it needs a forward net force just to keep moving at constant velocity. Correct the statement.

Answer / solution

Constant-velocity motion does not require a forward net force; zero net force is consistent with constant straight-line motion.

Compare inertia through mass, not through a separate “inertia force.” Rank a 1 kg mass and a 6 kg mass by inertia, then state the basis for your ranking.

Answer / solution

The 6 kg mass has greater inertia because inertia increases with mass.

Alignment / evidence

Learning Target: Students will explain Newton’s First Law and use the idea of inertia to predict whether an object’s motion will stay the same or change.

I Can: I can explain that inertia is a property of matter, not a force.

Representation: verbal explanation/context

Evidence job: U1-EP-0155 mapped to U1-MG02

Source basis: Framework approved Unit 1 force figures

Practice Set 1 12

U1-12-0156 · Practice Set 1 · 1.2 · U1-S2-IC2 · DOK 2 · inertia-property-not-force

A rider on a skateboard keeps moving after stepping off. Explain why saying ‘inertia keeps exerting a forward force’ is misleading.

Answer / solution

Inertia describes resistance to a change in velocity; continued motion with little net force does not require a forward force from inertia.

Alignment / evidence

Learning Target: Students will explain Newton’s First Law and use the idea of inertia to predict whether an object’s motion will stay the same or change.

I Can: I can explain that inertia is a property of matter, not a force.

Representation: verbal explanation/context

Evidence job: U1-EP-0156 mapped to U1-MG02

Source basis: Unit 1 Assessment Plan §1.2

Inertia—their tendency to resist a change in motion.

Practice Set 1 15

U1-12-0159 · Practice Set 1 · 1.2 · U1-S2-IC2 · DOK 2 · inertia-property-not-force

A heavy equipment case is harder to start moving and harder to stop than a light case. Explain this observation using inertia without inventing an ‘inertia force.’

Answer / solution

The heavier case has more mass and therefore more inertia, so a larger net force or more time is needed for the same change in motion.

Alignment / evidence

Learning Target: Students will explain Newton’s First Law and use the idea of inertia to predict whether an object’s motion will stay the same or change.

I Can: I can explain that inertia is a property of matter, not a force.

Practice Set 1 18

U1-12-0162 · Practice Set 1 · 1.2 · U1-S2-IC2 · DOK 2 · inertia-property-not-force

Compare inertia through mass, not through a separate “inertia force.” A student says, ‘Inertia pushed me forward when the car stopped.’ Rewrite the explanation so inertia is treated correctly.

Answer / solution

Inertia is the tendency of matter to resist changes in velocity; it is not a force pushing forward. The body tended to keep its previous motion while the car slowed.

Learning Target: Students will explain Newton’s First Law and use the idea of inertia to predict whether an object’s motion will stay the same or change.

Practice Set 1 19

U1-12-0163 · Practice Set 1 · 1.2 · U1-S2-IC3 · DOK 2 · force-identification-zero-net

List the actual interactions even when their vector sum is zero. The book in the diagram is at rest. Are there no forces acting, or is the net force zero? Identify the two shown forces.

Answer / solution

Forces are acting, but the net force is zero. The downward force is weight and the upward force is the table’s support force.

Alignment / evidence

Learning Target: Students will explain Newton’s First Law and use the idea of inertia to predict whether an object’s motion will stay the same or change.

I Can: I can distinguish between “no forces acting” and “no net force acting.” and identify support force, weight, and other common forces in simple situations.

Representation: force diagram / verbal context

Source basis: Hewitt §§2.3/2.6 Newton I/support-force source packet

Practice Set 3 1

U1-12-0193 · Practice Set 3 · 1.2 · U1-S2-IC1 · DOK 2 · newton-first-law-prediction

A rolling suitcase slows on a rough floor. Does this contradict Newton’s First Law? Explain.

Answer / solution

No. Friction provides a net force opposite the motion, so the velocity changes.

Alignment / evidence

Learning Target: Students will explain Newton’s First Law and use the idea of inertia to predict whether an object’s motion will stay the same or change.

I Can: I can state Newton’s First Law in everyday language.

Representation: verbal explanation/context

Evidence job: U1-EP-0193 mapped to U1-MG02

Source basis: Hewitt §§2.3/2.6 Newton I/support-force source packet

Practice Set 3 2

U1-12-0194 · Practice Set 3 · 1.2 · U1-S2-IC1 · DOK 2 · newton-first-law-prediction

A spacecraft coasts far from strong interactions after its engines shut off. Predict its motion using Newton’s First Law.

Answer / solution

It continues with essentially constant velocity as long as the net force remains negligible.

Alignment / evidence

Learning Target: Students will explain Newton’s First Law and use the idea of inertia to predict whether an object’s motion will stay the same or change.

I Can: I can state Newton’s First Law in everyday language.

Representation: verbal explanation/context

Practice Set 3 3

U1-12-0195 · Practice Set 3 · 1.2 · U1-S2-IC1 · DOK 2 · newton-first-law-prediction

State Newton’s First Law without using the word inertia, then connect your statement to unchanged velocity.

Answer / solution

If the net force is zero, an object’s velocity does not change: it stays at rest or continues at constant velocity in a straight line.

Alignment / evidence

Learning Target: Students will explain Newton’s First Law and use the idea of inertia to predict whether an object’s motion will stay the same or change.

I Can: I can state Newton’s First Law in everyday language.

Constant-velocity motion does not require a forward net force; zero net force is consistent with constant straight-line motion.

Practice Set 3 10

A loaded shopping cart and an empty cart move at the same speed. Which has greater inertia, and what property accounts for the difference?

The loaded cart; greater mass means greater inertia.

Alignment / evidence

Learning Target: Students will explain Newton’s First Law and use the idea of inertia to predict whether an object’s motion will stay the same or change.

Practice Set 3 11

U1-12-0203 · Practice Set 3 · 1.2 · U1-S2-IC2 · DOK 2 · inertia-property-not-force

Use mass to compare resistance to changes in motion. A student says, ‘Inertia pushed me forward when the car stopped.’ Rewrite the explanation so inertia is treated correctly.

Answer / solution

Inertia is the tendency of matter to resist changes in velocity; it is not a force pushing forward. The body tended to keep its previous motion while the car slowed.

Alignment / evidence

Learning Target: Students will explain Newton’s First Law and use the idea of inertia to predict whether an object’s motion will stay the same or change.

I Can: I can explain that inertia is a property of matter, not a force.

Practice Set 3 16

U1-12-0208 · Practice Set 3 · 1.2 · U1-S2-IC2 · DOK 2 · inertia-property-not-force

A heavy equipment case is harder to start moving and harder to stop than a light case. Explain this observation using inertia without inventing an ‘inertia force.’

The heavier case has more mass and therefore more inertia, so a larger net force or more time is needed for the same change in motion.

Practice Set 3 17

U1-12-0209 · Practice Set 3 · 1.2 · U1-S2-IC3 · DOK 2 · force-identification-zero-net

A sled rests on a level table. Name the downward and upward forces on it, then state whether ‘no forces act’ is correct.

Answer / solution

Weight acts downward and the table’s support force acts upward. ‘No forces act’ is incorrect; the forces can balance to zero net force.

Alignment / evidence

Learning Target: Students will explain Newton’s First Law and use the idea of inertia to predict whether an object’s motion will stay the same or change.

I Can: I can distinguish between “no forces acting” and “no net force acting.” and identify support force, weight, and other common forces in simple situations.

Representation: force diagram / verbal context

Source basis: Framework approved Unit 1 force figures

Practice Set 3 18

U1-12-0210 · Practice Set 3 · 1.2 · U1-S2-IC3 · DOK 2 · force-identification-zero-net

A hanging sign is motionless. Gravity pulls downward while the cord pulls upward. Explain why the situation can have zero net force without having zero forces.

Answer / solution

Both forces are present and opposite; if their magnitudes balance, their vector sum is zero.

Alignment / evidence

Learning Target: Students will explain Newton’s First Law and use the idea of inertia to predict whether an object’s motion will stay the same or change.

I Can: I can distinguish between “no forces acting” and “no net force acting.” and identify support force, weight, and other common forces in simple situations.

Forces are acting, but the net force is zero. The downward force is weight and the upward force is the table’s support force.

A suitcase rests on a level table. Name the downward and upward forces on it, then state whether ‘no forces act’ is correct.

Weight acts downward and the table’s support force acts upward. ‘No forces act’ is incorrect; the forces can balance to zero net force.

Alignment / evidence

Learning Target: Students will explain Newton’s First Law and use the idea of inertia to predict whether an object’s motion will stay the same or change.

Both forces are present and opposite; if their magnitudes balance, their vector sum is zero.

Answer / solution

The object at rest remains at rest; the moving object continues at constant velocity in a straight line.

Alignment / evidence

Learning Target: Students will explain Newton’s First Law and use the idea of inertia to predict whether an object’s motion will stay the same or change.

CYU 3

U1-12-0243 · CYU · 1.2 · U1-S2-IC2 · DOK 2 · inertia-property-not-force

A heavy equipment case is harder to start moving and harder to stop than a light case. Explain this observation using inertia without inventing an ‘inertia force.’

Answer / solution

The heavier case has more mass and therefore more inertia, so a larger net force or more time is needed for the same change in motion.

Alignment / evidence

Learning Target: Students will explain Newton’s First Law and use the idea of inertia to predict whether an object’s motion will stay the same or change.

I Can: I can explain that inertia is a property of matter, not a force.

Representation: verbal explanation/context

Evidence job: U1-EP-0243 mapped to U1-MG02

Source basis: Unit 1 Assessment Plan §1.2

CYU 4

U1-12-0244 · CYU · 1.2 · U1-S2-IC2 · DOK 2 · inertia-property-not-force

Explain resistance to velocity change without inventing a new force. A student says, ‘Inertia pushed me forward when the car stopped.’ Rewrite the explanation so inertia is treated correctly.

Answer / solution

Inertia is the tendency of matter to resist changes in velocity; it is not a force pushing forward. The body tended to keep its previous motion while the car slowed.

Alignment / evidence

Learning Target: Students will explain Newton’s First Law and use the idea of inertia to predict whether an object’s motion will stay the same or change.

I Can: I can explain that inertia is a property of matter, not a force.

Representation: verbal explanation/context

Source basis: Hewitt §§2.3/2.6 Newton I/support-force source packet

U1-12-0269 · Exit Ticket C · 1.2 · U1-S2-IC2 · DOK 2 · inertia-property-not-force

Keep inertia in the model as a property, not a push or pull. Rank a 1 kg mass and a 6 kg mass by inertia, then state the basis for your ranking.

Answer / solution

The 6 kg mass has greater inertia because inertia increases with mass.

Alignment / evidence

Learning Target: Students will explain Newton’s First Law and use the idea of inertia to predict whether an object’s motion will stay the same or change.

I Can: I can explain that inertia is a property of matter, not a force.

Representation: verbal explanation/context

Evidence job: U1-EP-0269 mapped to U1-MG02

Source basis: Framework approved Unit 1 force figures

Exit Ticket C 4

U1-12-0270 · Exit Ticket C · 1.2 · U1-S2-IC1 · DOK 2 · newton-first-law-prediction

It remains at rest unless a nonzero net force acts.

Alignment / evidence

Learning Target: Students will explain Newton’s First Law and use the idea of inertia to predict whether an object’s motion will stay the same or change.

Section 1.3: Net Force and Vectors

Learning Target: Students will represent forces as vectors and determine the direction and relative size of the net force in one-dimensional and simple two-dimensional situations.

WTC

WTC 1

U1-13-0271 · WTC · 1.3 · U1-S3-IC3 · DOK 3 · wtc-shared-physics-context

Three students pull a low-friction cart: two pull to the right and one pulls to the left. Sketch or describe force arrows that show both magnitude and direction, explain what makes force a vector, and determine how you would decide the resultant direction before doing arithmetic.

Answer / solution

Force arrows encode magnitude and direction. Forces in the same direction reinforce; opposing forces subtract vectorially. The resultant points toward the larger total directed force.

Alignment / evidence

Learning Target: Students will represent forces as vectors and determine the direction and relative size of the net force in one-dimensional and simple two-dimensional situations.

I Can: I can identify the resultant force from a simple vector diagram and use arrow length and direction to compare force strength and direction.

Representation: phenomenon + verbal/model reasoning

Evidence job: U1-EP-0271 mapped to U1-MG03

Source basis: Hewitt §2.4 net-force/vector source packet

Notes Example

Notes Example 1

U1-13-0272 · Notes Example · 1.3 · U1-S3-IC1 · DOK 2 · force-vector-meaning

Explain why reversing the direction of a force changes the vector even if its magnitude stays the same.

Answer / solution

Direction is part of the vector; equal magnitudes in opposite directions are different vectors.

Alignment / evidence

Learning Target: Students will represent forces as vectors and determine the direction and relative size of the net force in one-dimensional and simple two-dimensional situations.

I Can: I can explain why force is a vector quantity.

Its direction and its length, which converts to magnitude using the scale.

Section 1.4: Equilibrium and Balanced Motion

Learning Target: Students will determine whether an object is in mechanical equilibrium and explain how balanced forces relate to rest or constant straight-line motion.

WTC

WTC 1

U1-14-0406 · WTC · 1.4 · U1-S4-IC3 · DOK 3 · wtc-shared-physics-context

Compare two systems: a hanging sign that is motionless and a cart that travels straight at constant speed. For each, describe what must be true about net force. Then explain why one is static equilibrium and the other can be dynamic equilibrium even though forces still act.

Answer / solution

Both can have zero net force. The sign is static equilibrium because it is at rest; the cart is dynamic equilibrium because it has constant straight-line velocity. Forces may be present but balanced.

Alignment / evidence

Learning Target: Students will determine whether an object is in mechanical equilibrium and explain how balanced forces relate to rest or constant straight-line motion.

I Can: I can explain why an object moving at constant speed in a straight line can be in equilibrium and use the equilibrium rule to reason about upward/downward and left/right forces.

Representation: phenomenon + verbal/model reasoning

Evidence job: U1-EP-0406 mapped to U1-MG03

Source basis: Hewitt §§2.5/2.7 equilibrium source packet

Notes Example

Notes Example 1

U1-14-0407 · Notes Example · 1.4 · U1-S4-IC1 · DOK 2 · static-dynamic-equilibrium

A moving walkway carries a suitcase in a straight line at constant velocity with zero net force on the suitcase. Why can this be equilibrium even though it is moving?

Answer / solution

Equilibrium requires zero net force, not zero velocity; constant-velocity motion is dynamic equilibrium.

Alignment / evidence

Learning Target: Students will determine whether an object is in mechanical equilibrium and explain how balanced forces relate to rest or constant straight-line motion.

I Can: I can recognize static equilibrium and dynamic equilibrium.

Representation: verbal explanation/context

Evidence job: U1-EP-0407 mapped to U1-MG02

Source basis: Framework U1 equilibrium figures

Notes Example 2

U1-14-0409 · Notes Example · 1.4 · U1-S4-IC2 · DOK 2 · rest-with-balanced-forces

A motionless object can still have interacting forces acting on it. A sign sits motionless on a horizontal surface. A classmate says, ‘Since it is not moving, gravity has turned off.’ Identify the error and name the balancing interaction.

Answer / solution

Gravity still acts as weight. The surface provides an upward support force that can balance the weight.

Alignment / evidence

Learning Target: Students will determine whether an object is in mechanical equilibrium and explain how balanced forces relate to rest or constant straight-line motion.

I Can: I can explain why an object at rest can still have forces acting on it.

U1-14-0433 · Practice Set 1 · 1.4 · U1-S4-IC3 · DOK 2 · equilibrium-rule-constant-motion

Constant straight-line velocity requires zero resultant force. Both signs are motionless. What must be true about the vector sum of all forces on each sign, even though the support arrangements differ?

Answer / solution

The net force on each sign must be zero.

Alignment / evidence

Learning Target: Students will determine whether an object is in mechanical equilibrium and explain how balanced forces relate to rest or constant straight-line motion.

I Can: I can explain why an object moving at constant speed in a straight line can be in equilibrium and use the equilibrium rule to reason about upward/downward and left/right forces.

Representation: force diagram / equilibrium relationship

Evidence job: U1-EP-0433 mapped to U1-MG03

Source basis: Hewitt §§2.5/2.7 equilibrium source packet

Practice Set 1 20

U1-14-0434 · Practice Set 1 · 1.4 · U1-S4-IC3 · DOK 2 · equilibrium-rule-constant-motion

Constant straight-line velocity requires zero resultant force. The box moves to the right at constant speed. What friction force is required for horizontal equilibrium, and why?

Answer / solution

60 N to the left, because constant straight-line velocity requires zero horizontal net force.

Static equilibrium is at rest; dynamic equilibrium is constant-velocity straight-line motion.

Practice Set 2 9

Gravity still acts as weight. The surface provides an upward support force that can balance the weight.

Section 1.5: Modeling Forces in the Real World

Learning Target: Students will create and critique force models for real-world situations involving inertia, support force, net force, and equilibrium.

WTC

WTC 1

U1-15-0541 · WTC · 1.5 · U1-S5-IC3 · DOK 3 · wtc-shared-physics-context

A delivery cart rolls straight at constant speed after a worker stops actively accelerating it. A proposed force model shows weight downward, support force upward, and a large forward horizontal force with no backward force. Critique the model using the motion evidence, identify a revision, and explain what the corrected net force predicts about the cart’s motion.

Answer / solution

Constant straight-line velocity requires zero net force. The horizontal model is inconsistent; either the forward force should be removed or a balancing backward interaction included. The corrected model should have zero resultant and predict unchanged velocity.

Alignment / evidence

Learning Target: Students will create and critique force models for real-world situations involving inertia, support force, net force, and equilibrium.

I Can: I can explain how the net force affects the object’s motion and critique an incorrect force explanation and revise it using physics vocabulary.

Representation: phenomenon + verbal/model reasoning

Evidence job: U1-EP-0541 mapped to U1-MG04

Source basis: Hewitt §§2.3–2.7 synthesis source packet

Notes Example 3

U1-15-0546 · Notes Example · 1.5 · U1-S5-IC3 · DOK 3 · critique-force-explanation

Check the proposed model against Newton’s First Law before revising it. A student explains an equipment case that speeds up to the right by saying, ‘Its inertia force became larger.’ Critique the explanation and replace it with one using net force correctly.

Answer / solution

Inertia is not a force. Speeding up to the right requires a nonzero net force to the right; the change in motion is linked to that resultant force.

Practice Set 1 11

U1-15-0560 · Practice Set 1 · 1.5 · U1-S5-IC2 · DOK 2 · balanced-unbalanced-model

Compare the vector sum of forces with the stated motion evidence. The figure states that the crate moves right at constant speed. Are the drawn horizontal forces balanced or unbalanced, and does the model agree with the motion description?

Answer / solution

The forces are unbalanced: 80 N right and 40 N left give 40 N right. That does not agree with constant straight-line velocity, which requires zero net force.

Alignment / evidence

Learning Target: Students will create and critique force models for real-world situations involving inertia, support force, net force, and equilibrium.

Practice Set 1 18

U1-15-0567 · Practice Set 1 · 1.5 · U1-S5-IC3 · DOK 3 · critique-force-explanation

Replace any inertia-as-force claim with a net-force explanation. A student explains a box that speeds up to the right by saying, ‘Its inertia force became larger.’ Critique the explanation and replace it with one using net force correctly.

Answer / solution

Inertia is not a force. Speeding up to the right requires a nonzero net force to the right; the change in motion is linked to that resultant force.

Alignment / evidence

Learning Target: Students will create and critique force models for real-world situations involving inertia, support force, net force, and equilibrium.

I Can: I can explain how the net force affects the object’s motion and critique an incorrect force explanation and revise it using physics vocabulary.

Practice Set 1 20

U1-15-0569 · Practice Set 1 · 1.5 · U1-S5-IC3 · DOK 3 · critique-force-explanation

Check the proposed model against Newton’s First Law before revising it. The motion description says constant speed in a straight line, but the force model has a nonzero rightward resultant. Explain the mismatch and state one revision that would make the model consistent.

Answer / solution

Constant velocity requires zero net force. The model should be revised so the opposing horizontal forces balance, or the motion description must indicate changing velocity.

Alignment / evidence

Practice Set 1 21

U1-15-0570 · Practice Set 1 · 1.5 · U1-S5-IC3 · DOK 3 · critique-force-explanation

Check the proposed model against Newton’s First Law before revising it. The delivery cart rolls at constant speed, but the diagram shows only a forward force. Critique the explanation ‘the forward force is what keeps it moving’ and revise the model-based explanation.

Answer / solution

Constant straight-line motion is consistent with zero net force. The diagram is incomplete or inconsistent; a balancing backward force such as friction/drag should be included if a forward force is present. Inertia is not a forward force.

Extra Practice 8

The forces are unbalanced: 80 N right and 40 N left give 40 N right. That does not agree with constant straight-line velocity, which requires zero net force.

Extra Practice 16

U1-15-0637 · Extra Practice · 1.5 · U1-S5-IC3 · DOK 3 · critique-force-explanation

Revise the explanation so the force model and motion state agree. A student explains a box that speeds up to the right by saying, ‘Its inertia force became larger.’ Critique the explanation and replace it with one using net force correctly.

Answer / solution

Inertia is not a force. Speeding up to the right requires a nonzero net force to the right; the change in motion is linked to that resultant force.

Alignment / evidence

Constant velocity requires zero net force. The model should be revised so the opposing horizontal forces balance, or the motion description must indicate changing velocity.

Constant straight-line motion is consistent with zero net force. The diagram is incomplete or inconsistent; a balancing backward force such as friction/drag should be included if a forward force is present. Inertia is not a forward force.

V2 Question 7

U1-12-0702 · Secure Summative · 1.2 · U1-S2-IC3 · DOK 2 · force-identification-zero-net

The person in the diagram at the North Hall demonstration remains motionless. Explain why this is a zero-net-force situation rather than a no-force situation, naming the two forces.

Answer / solution

Weight acts downward and the scale/support force acts upward. They are equal and opposite, so the resultant is zero although both forces are present.

Alignment / evidence

Learning Target: Students will explain Newton’s First Law and use the idea of inertia to predict whether an object’s motion will stay the same or change.

I Can: I can distinguish between “no forces acting” and “no net force acting.” and identify support force, weight, and other common forces in simple situations.

The book shown at the North Hall demonstration remains at rest. Explain how the diagram disproves the claim ‘an object at rest has no forces acting on it.’

Answer / solution

The downward weight and upward support force both act. They balance to a zero resultant, allowing the book to remain at rest.

Alignment / evidence

Learning Target: Students will determine whether an object is in mechanical equilibrium and explain how balanced forces relate to rest or constant straight-line motion.

I Can: I can explain why an object at rest can still have forces acting on it.

  2. Inertia acts upward to cancel gravity.

  4. No forces act because the book is at rest.
Answer / solution

Correct choice: C

Weight and support force act, and their net can be zero.

Alignment / evidence

Learning Target: Students will explain Newton’s First Law and use the idea of inertia to predict whether an object’s motion will stay the same or change.

I Can: I can distinguish between “no forces acting” and “no net force acting.” and identify support force, weight, and other common forces in simple situations.

Representation: force diagram / verbal context

V6 Question 1

U1-11-0776 · Secure Summative · 1.1 · U1-S1-IC3 · DOK 3 · evidence-model-meaning

At the Summit classroom, repeated measurements are 3.8 s, 3.9 s, 3.8 s, 4.0 s, and 3.9 s. A model predicts about 3.9 s. Evaluate how well the evidence supports the model and explain what a physics relationship contributes beyond producing a number.

Answer / solution

The measurements cluster around 3.9 s, so the model is supported for these conditions. A relationship communicates how physical quantities are connected and the assumptions/meaning of that connection, not only a calculation.

Alignment / evidence

Learning Target: Students will explain how physics uses observation, measurement, evidence, models, and testable claims to understand the natural world.
